On Wednesday, June 26, 2013 10:00:36 PM UTC-4, Mike Lawrence wrote:
Ah! One big speedup can be achieved by not re-using variables inside the model block. I was initialized a variable, setting its value, then later re-setting its value to something else. On a hunch I tried initializing two variables and setting the value to each once, and this runs far faster.

I would be surprised if something like that made any difference. In your R code, you have

set.seed(1)

but that doesn't actually affect Stan. To be replicable, you need to pass a seed to the seed argument of stan().

My guess is that your model is such that if you get good starting values, it adapts and runs decently. And if you get bad starting values, then it doesn't.

Ben

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Help with optimization?
parts:
Here are a couple tips to speed things up:

- Compute 1-accuracy[i] and reuse it instead of recomputing it 3 times
- As above, for many of the computations in that loop they are the same for each subject.  Precompute them for each subject in an array and then reference them in the loop.
- If L is large, instead of incrementing lp__ each time, create a vector[2*L] lpterms and set it's entry in the loop.  Then at the end of the loop write: lp__ <- lp__ + sum(lpterms);

The last one is probably your best bet for a quick win.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Help with optimization?
parts:
On 6/26/13 10:16 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Wednesday, June 26, 2013 10:00:36 PM UTC-4, Mike Lawrence wrote:
>
> Ah! One big speedup can be achieved by not re-using variables inside the model block. I was initialized a variable,
> setting its value, then later re-setting its value to something else. On a hunch I tried initializing two variables
> and setting the value to each once, and this runs far faster.
>
>
> I would be surprised if something like that made any difference.

I think that depends on how bad the original program was :-)

For instance, this is slow:

vector[K] temp;
for (...) {
temp <- some calc for b;
... use temp ...
temp <- some calc for c;
... use temp ...
}

but this is faster:

vector[K] b;
b <- some calc for b;
vector[K] c;
c <- some calc for c;
for (...) {
... use b ...
... use c ...
}

There shouldn't be a noticeable difference between:

vector[K] temp;
temp <- some calc for b;
... use b ...
temp <- some calc for c;
... use c ...

and

vector[K] b;
b <- some calc for b;
vector[K] c;
c <- some calc for c;
... use b ...
... use c ...

In general, you want to define things that are used multiple
times as high up as possible.

- Bob

Never rule out the possibility that it's not the speed
of the iterations that's too slow, but the parameterization
or the model itself. Alas, these are much more involved and
subtle problems to fix.

You are running at -O3, right? If not, doing that's your
biggest win.

- Bob
